chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Ali ibn Asbat from a man from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

When the month of Ramadan enters, there is a condition for God in it. God Almighty said: 'So whoever among you witnesses the month, let him fast it.' A man may not leave (his home) when Ramadan enters except for Hajj or Umrah, or for wealth he fears will be lost, or for a brother he fears will perish. And he may not leave for the destruction of his brother's wealth. So when the night of the twenty-third passes, let him go wherever he wishes.

And whenever he leaves based on the types of travel we mentioned, breaking the fast becomes obligatory upon him. This is indicated by God's saying: 'So whoever among you witnesses the month, let him fast it; and whoever is ill or on a journey, then an equal number of other days.' Thus, He made fasting obligatory by the apparent meaning of the wording for whoever witnesses the month, and prescribed making up (the fasts) explicitly for whoever is ill or traveling. If breaking the fast were not obligatory, then making up an equal number of days would not be obligatory upon him.
And what we have narrated also indicates the obligation of breaking the fast.
ai.seo_question: What are the conditions under which a traveler must break their fast during Ramadan according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* establishes the principle that travel during Ramadan necessitates obligatory breaking of the fast (*wajib al-iftar*), rather than mere permission, based on the logical implication of the Quranic verse requiring makeup days for travelers. It specifies that departure is restricted to the first twenty-three nights for valid causes such as Hajj, Umrah, preserving wealth, or visiting family, after which one is free to leave. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly view that the obligation to make up fasts confirms the prior obligation to break them during the journey.
